I wrote up the full picture on Mamuka, who he was, how he ended up at Winn, what ICE's own data says, and what the new death-reporting policy change means. Full analysis here:
austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

The same day Mamuka died, ICE's acting director signed a memo ending the requirement to report deaths that occur within 30 days of a person's release from custody. Mamuka died inside, so he's counted but going forward, others might not  be.

Last week, a DHS Inspector General report found unsafe conditions, unsanitary food storage, and missing use-of-force documentation at Winn Correctional, the same facility where Mamuka died. Although We can't establish a direct link, we can definitely see the pattern.

Using ICE's national average daily detention rate of $150, taxpayers spent roughly $17,850 holding him for those 119 days. There is no evidence in the record that his detention served any public safety or national security purpose.

His arrest happened under an ICE operation targeting commercial truck drivers. Of the more than 1,350 arrests tied to that operation, roughly 7 in 10 involved people with no criminal record, the same classification ICE gave Mamuka.

ICE couldn't deport him. He had a case pending before an immigration judge and no final removal order. He was classified at the lowest detention risk level, there was no mandatory detention requirement and he had no prior detainers.
ICE's own data shows he had no criminal history. He wasn't even the target of his arrest, he was picked up as a collateral, meaning he just happened to be nearby when ICE arrested someone else.
